title: Laying on hands (Luke 4:31–44)
hookLine: at sunset they bring the sick, and he lays his hands on every one

lines: WAITING FOR THE SUN TO GO DOWN.
cards: Capernaum, a city of Galilee. The day began on the sabbath, with Jesus teaching in the synagogue. Now the sun is going down, and the streets start to fill.
Luke doesn't say why the crowd waits for sunset; some readers connect it with the sabbath, which ends at sundown. Mats, stretchers, people leaning on cousins' shoulders, children being carried.
Everyone with someone sick is heading to the same door, the house of a man named Simon.

teach.h: HOLD THY PEACE, AND COME OUT.
teach.b: The day began in the synagogue, where a man possessed by an unclean spirit cried out, and Jesus said: "Hold thy peace, and come out of him." People were stunned: "What a word is this!"
Then, at Simon's house, Simon's mother-in-law lay "taken with a great fever."

teach.h: THE FEVER LEFT; SHE ROSE AND SERVED.
teach.b: Luke, whom tradition remembers as a physician, says Jesus "stood over her, and rebuked the fever; and it left her: and immediately she arose and ministered unto them." She gets up and serves the table.

teach.h: AT SUNSET, HANDS ON EVERY ONE.
teach.b: Then sunset, and the verse behind today's title: "Now when the sun was setting, all they that had any sick with divers diseases brought them unto him; and he laid his hands on every one of them, and healed them."
Every one of them. Not a wave from the doorway, not a blessing in bulk. Hands on each person, one by one.
Laying on hands was an old gesture in Israel's scriptures, for blessing and for setting someone apart.

Christians kept it: in ordination, in confirmation in some churches, and in prayer for the sick, from Catholic and Orthodox anointing to Pentecostal healing services. Then, at dawn, Jesus slips away to a deserted place.
The crowds find him and beg him to stay.
He says: "I must preach the kingdom of God to other cities also: for therefore am I sent."

teach.h: HE LAID HIS HANDS ON EVERY ONE OF THEM.
teach.b: Full attention to each person at night. In the morning, he moves on, because, he says, that is what he was sent for.

how: Churches lay hands on people in ordination, some in confirmation, and in prayer for the sick, including the Catholic and Orthodox anointing of the sick and healing prayer in Pentecostal and charismatic churches.

the city where the high priest Caiaphas lived

games.q: it's dawn. last night a whole town came to you, and now they're begging you to stay. what do you do?
o: go to other cities too: that's what you were sent for.
games.why: he says he must preach the kingdom of God to other cities also. full attention at night, freedom to leave in the morning.

practice: Picture that doorway at sunset, the line of people, and one pair of hands, one person at a time.

Then bring to mind someone who usually gets the half of you that's looking at a screen, a child, a partner, a parent on the phone, a coworker, and picture giving them all of you for five minutes: eyes up, phone away, listening to the end of their sentences.
If you pray, hold that person before God; if not, hold them in mind with care.

wordCard.voice: Capernaum. The city where, at sunset, Jesus laid his hands on every sick person brought to Simon's door, one by one.

orig.note: Greek: a laying on. the noun in Acts 8:18 and Hebrews 6:2; Luke 4:40 uses the verb.

carryVoice: Your line: every one of them. A week of a boy in the temple, a crowd at the river, a desert, a hometown and a doorway at sunset. Seven days, done.
